turn_text: Thank you. Thank you for having me.

Let me ask you about your view of the House Agriculture Committee. You are from an urban district in Ohio and you sit on that committee. Do you feel like that it is a place that you can have a positive input and impact on this farm bill?

Absolutely. You know, people do think it's a little odd that I'm from Cleveland and I sit on the committee. But let me just suggest to you that I am excited about the opportunity to give a different view from what they, under normal circumstances, would get that the committee has historically been very farm-based. And I think that when you look at agriculture, it encompasses so many more things. So I'm just happy to be a part of broadening the perspective and the discussion about what kinds of things we can do with the farm bill.

The Farm Bill as the House Agriculture Committee passed it apparently wasn't what you wanted as it shows that you voted against that. Could you tell me what it was about the bill that made you vote no? I

voted against it and I spoke against it as well. One of the major issues for me clearly was a $16 billion cut to SNAP as well as the change in the eligibility requirements to qualify for SNAP. And there were some other things as well, certainly as it relates to 1890 institutions and other things, but in particular, my biggest concern was that you cannot, in this economy, cut $16 billion from SNAP. So that was my biggest issue with the bill.

You had some allies in that there were some Republicans who felt like there weren't nearly enough cuts to SNAP to the point that Congressman Holskamp was kicked off the committee for this coming term i wonder what that shows of extremes on both sides and uh... both of you uh... not wanting to let a bill like this go through

well uh... let me just first say that i don't believe that the congressman was was removed from the committee because he voted against the farm bill i think that was a wholly different situation with a different message uh... but more importantly you're right but there is has been a lot of discussion that uh... that the SNAP pieces or the nutrition pieces need to be separated from the farm bill and look that differently. But because it is not that way right now, the only way that we can address the situation is to vote against it. Yes, there are people that think that it wasn't enough cuts, but let me just suggest to you this. The Senate only cut $4.5 billion out of there in their bill for SNAP. We turn around and do $16 billion. When you look at the fact that almost 8% of the US population is unemployed, and that the current poverty rate is the second highest has been in 45 years. You can't talk about not feeding hungry children and hungry families. And when you look at the effects of SNAP, about 75% of all SNAP recipients are families with young children. And the other 25% are seniors or people with disabilities. So what is it that we are to do? Are we to say that as a nation, We are going to refuse to feed hungry people. We just say as a nation that we are not concerned about the nutrition of our children. I don't think that people understand the consequences of making those kinds of decisions unless they live in environments like mine.
